name: Electrolyte protocol

lead: The electrolyte protocol is a routine of deliberately taking sodium, potassium, magnesium and related minerals, often with water, in the hope of debloating. The appearance goal is less facial puffiness and a tighter, leaner look.

In looksmaxxing circles the term is linked to a long mineral-balancing program posted on looksmax.org by a user called Gbolduev, which was originally written in 2012 and links mineral status to fatigue and other conditions. Medical literature describes structured electrolyte protocols in clinics, such as a pharmacist-managed potassium and magnesium protocol for patients on heart-rhythm drugs.

paras: Practitioners add electrolyte drinks or mineral supplements and adjust salt intake as part of a daily routine. The forum program also includes daily detox steps and recommends a hair mineral test to see which cofactors are needed. Timelines are not specified in the sources.

The forum author himself notes that minerals can push body chemistry in different directions quickly and could be dangerous without understanding. Clinical protocols base potassium and magnesium dosing on measured blood levels. People with heart or kidney conditions are generally advised by clinicians to use supplements only under medical care.

angle.text: Because water balance follows sodium and other electrolytes, people use mineral routines to manage bloat and puffiness. The look sought is a tighter, drier face and midsection.

lead: The electrolyte protocol is a looksmaxxing routine centred on salt and minerals such as sodium, potassium and magnesium. People use it to reduce bloat and puffiness, working toward a leaner, more defined face and body.[1]

A looksmax.org thread presents a mineral-balancing program by user Gbolduev, which the post says dates from 2012 and was largely unchanged since. It is framed for people with chronic fatigue and other conditions, and it includes daily detox procedures and a recommendation to get a hair mineral test before choosing cofactors.[1]

In clinical medicine, electrolyte protocols exist as well. A 2017 evaluation of a pharmacist-managed protocol aimed to keep serum potassium at 4.0 to 5.0 mmol/L in patients on antiarrhythmic drugs using dietary advice plus magnesium and potassium supplementation.[2]

paras: The label covers any structured routine of taking electrolytes. Forum versions bundle mineral intake with detox steps and with testing to identify imbalances, with the author arguing the program is not specific to one person.[1]

Oral rehydration references explain the physiology behind such routines: sodium absorption is coupled to glucose, and water follows sodium across the gut, with potassium helping prevent low levels; sports drinks are described there as less optimal than oral rehydration solutions.[3]

The forum author attributes many problems to mineral imbalances and writes that stress, alcohol and mineral deficiencies can cause protein deficiency and pancreatic insufficiency. He cautions that minerals can move body chemistry fast and could be dangerous for those without experience.[1] Another poster collated his writings into notes, saying his posts are scattered and hard to piece together.[1]

A pharmacist-managed protocol at Ohio State's antiarrhythmic clinic used diet advice and magnesium and potassium supplements to keep serum potassium within target in outpatients, with levels measured by blood tests.[2] This is a medical protocol for a defined patient group, not a cosmetic one.
No studies found on electrolyte routines for appearance or debloating. The clinical protocol study above concerns patients on heart-rhythm medication.[2]
